A1.justification: Both PDFs describe EmoEditor and the EmoPair dataset. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and supplementary material are readable and support comparison despite substantial revisions and reformatting.

before.justification: v2 reports original image-generation experiments, quantitative comparisons, ablations, and online and in-lab human preference studies.

after.justification: v4 reports original image-generation results, human preference studies, component ablations, human region annotations, and CrossTest evaluation.

M1.justification: In Section 3.2, v2 encodes the target emotion alone and retains that embedding during iterative inference. v4 encodes the target minus the predicted source-emotion distribution and updates this direction after each iteration. Acceptance thresholds also change from SSIM 0.3–0.8 and emotion confidence above 0.8 to SSIM 0.5–0.8 and confidence above 0.6. The dual-branch backbone and alignment loss remain.

E1.justification: EmoPair training, EmoSet evaluation, within-valence editing, and neutral MSCOCO examples are retained. v4 additionally demonstrates multi-emotion editing by adding a second target emotion of the same valence, introducing a distinct output requirement in Figure 7(c).

E2.justification: The main quantitative and human comparisons expand from five baselines to nine, adding CtrlNet, SDEdit, AIF, and EmoEdit alongside CT, NST, Csty, Ip2p, and LMS. LMS itself changes from BLIP plus GPT-3 plus Ip2p to GPT-4o plus the model called GPT-o4 in v4 plus Ip2p.

E3.justification: v4 replaces EMR, ESR, ENRD, and ESS with CAM-based and human-annotation-based ESMI. It adds human region annotation and CrossTest using predictors trained on disjoint EmoSet subsets. The reported online study changes from 417 participants with 100 trials each to 136 with 180 each, while the ten-person in-lab study disappears. v2 already reports 2,016 cross-valence result pairs; v4's 2,016 count alone does not establish an enlarged test set.

E4.justification: v4 expands the two component-removal ablations into seven configurations testing text versus emotion encodings, source-to-target direction, iterative inference, and alignment loss (Table 2). It adds human checks of emotion-region localization and CrossTest analysis of evaluator bias. Conversely, v2's iteration-count sweep and online-versus-in-lab consistency analysis are removed, and failure examples are revised.

E5.justification: Both versions identify human-preference error bars as standard errors. Neither reports model-run seeds, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests. Changed participant counts and additional plots do not establish a different uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: The principal numerical results are replaced under revised methods and protocols: v2 reports 50.20% EMR and 92.86% ESR, whereas v4 reports 51.56% CAM-based ESMI and 49.99% HA-based ESMI. Figure 5's preference over Ip2p changes from 61% to 68% in the revised study. New CrossTest results rank NST first at 45.35 and EmoEditor second at 43.95. These are not comparable-metric performance gains. v4 also contains conflicting EmoEdit scores: 32.94 in Table 1 versus 39.24 in Table S1.

T1.justification: The mathematical evaluation framework changes substantially. v4 defines ESMI as an equal-weight combination of normalized, clipped KL-distance improvement and the proportion of regional image changes occurring in emotion-evoking areas, replacing the four separate metric definitions in v2. This changes substantive mathematical definitions, although the diffusion and alignment losses remain and neither version presents theorem-and-proof results.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and discussion redefine the evaluation contribution from four new metrics to one metric balancing emotional evocation and structural preservation. The principal claims about the task, dual-branch EmoEditor, approximately 340,000-pair dataset, instruction-free inference, and superiority over competitors otherwise remain.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive interpretation of source-aware editing and evaluator weaknesses, especially CrossTest's finding that color-sensitive predictors can favor NST's overlays. It also discusses excitement-specific difficulty, limits of the eight-category emotion taxonomy, and LMS applicability constraints. Conversely, v2's explicit limitation about preserving structure while changing semantic identity, illustrated by a tiger becoming coastal rocks, is removed.

D1.justification: v4 provides a GitHub link and reports code, model, and dataset availability, replacing v2's promise of future release. It newly documents same-emotion pair filtering, three-annotator review of 300 images and subsequent subset fine-tuning, and the 46-participant region-annotation procedure. These expand reproducibility information; the basic Ip2p initialization, ADAM optimizer, A5000 hardware, and 1,000 diffusion steps are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 updates the existing positioning with discussion of SDEdit, PnP, CtrlNet, and EmoEdit, including a specific contrast with EmoEdit's fixed learned queries. It expands discussion of the already-cited AIF and updates citations supporting LMS. The overarching positioning around end-to-end emotional understanding and local/global editing remains.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, results, and discussion undergo substantial rewriting and condensation. Quantitative and qualitative cross-valence results are consolidated, supplementary experimental subsections are reordered, references move after the supplement, and the NeurIPS checklist is removed. These are substantial narrative and organizational changes beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v4 adopts a two-column main text, updates architecture diagrams, replaces and rearranges qualitative montages, and adds per-image ESMI labels. It restructures the main comparison table, separates ablations into Table 2, and adds region-annotation figures and a CrossTest table. Retained dataset examples are compressed into side-by-side displays, while human-result displays lose their in-lab panels.

improvement.justification: Expanded baselines, source-conditioning ablations, human-region checks, and CrossTest strengthen scrutiny of the method and address v2's acknowledged evaluator-bias concern. Reported resource access also improves reproducibility. These gains are tempered by removal of the in-lab and iteration-sensitivity analyses, conflicting EmoEdit scores in Tables 1 and S1, and retained broad superiority language despite NST winning CrossTest. The net improvement is supported but limited by these evidential and reporting weaknesses.
